notes: The phrase can refer to Paul remembering the Philippians or to their remembrance of him.
‘You’ is plural. ‘Among you’ may also be rendered ‘in you.’ In verse 7, ‘I hold you in my heart’ can also be read ‘you hold me in your heart.’
The Greek word can denote the imperial guard or a governor’s headquarters. The text does not name the place of imprisonment.
‘Salvation’ can also mean deliverance or vindication; the following verses keep both life and death in view.
The verb means to live or conduct oneself as a citizen. It is related to ‘citizenship’ in 3:20. ‘One spirit’ may refer to a shared disposition or to the Spirit.
vocabulary: Slave; Paul and Timothy use the term of their relation to Christ.
Internal organs, used figuratively for deep affection.

notes: The abbreviated Greek can describe Christ’s way of thinking or the mindset that is yours in Christ.
‘Something to exploit’ can also be understood as ‘something to grasp or seize.’ The main text retains ‘form of God’ and ‘equality with God.’
The text says ‘emptied himself’ without naming something he emptied himself of. The following phrases describe taking a slave’s form and becoming human.
The commands and ‘you’ are plural, addressed to the community. ‘In you’ can also mean ‘among you.’
‘Holding firmly to’ can also mean ‘holding out.’
‘Messenger’ renders apostolos, someone sent or commissioned; here he is sent by the Philippians.
vocabulary: Think, adopt a mindset or set one’s mind; a recurring verb in the letter.
Form; used of both God and a slave.
Be poured out as a drink offering.

notes: ‘Mutilation’ and ‘circumcision’ form a Greek wordplay. The text does not name the targets of the harsh warning more precisely here.
The word rendered ‘refuse’ can refer to rubbish, discarded scraps or excrement. It is strongly dismissive.
The Greek phrase can mean ‘Christ’s faithfulness’ or ‘faith in Christ.’ The following phrase separately names faith as the basis of righteousness from God.
‘Because Christ has taken hold of me’ can also be understood in terms of purpose: ‘for which Christ took hold of me.’ The pinned text names Christ without adding Jesus here.
‘Made perfect’ and ‘mature’ translate forms of the same word-family.
The pinned Greek has the shorter command without the additional phrases about a rule and a shared mindset found in some witnesses.
vocabulary: Loss, including an accounting loss; contrasted with gain.
Take hold of, grasp or attain.

notes: The appeal is repeated equally for Euodia and Syntyche. Both women are described as sharing in the work of the good news. The ‘true companion’ is not named unambiguously; the Greek can also be read as a personal name, Syzygos.
‘Near’ may refer to presence, time or both.
Literally, ‘I have strength for all things in the one strengthening me.’ The preceding verse names plenty, hunger and need. The pinned Greek does not add the name Christ in this verse.
Giving, receiving, account and receipt language forms a connected accounting image. Verse 17 combines it with the image of fruit.
‘Your’ addresses the community; ‘spirit’ is singular. The pinned text ends without an added Amen.
vocabulary: Be initiated or learn a secret.
